presentingComplaint: Progressive drowsiness and confusion over 5 days with marked polyuria and polydipsia
history: 5-day history of increasing thirst, frequent large-volume urination and worsening lethargy, now barely rousable. Poor oral intake for 2 days after a recent chest infection treated with a short course of steroids. Type 2 diabetes for 12 years on metformin and gliclazide with poor adherence; lives alone with limited fluid access. No history of ketone-prone diabetes, alcohol, or overdose. No abdominal pain or vomiting.
examination: Profoundly dehydrated: dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, sunken eyes, prolonged capillary refill. GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5), no focal neurological deficit and no meningism. No Kussmaul respiration and no acetone on breath. No focus of sepsis on examination; chest clear, abdomen soft and non-tender.
imaging: Chest X-ray clear; CT head not indicated in absence of focal deficit - obtundation attributable to hyperosmolality
microbiology: Blood and urine cultures sent to exclude precipitating infection; results pending, no clinical focus
citations: Harrison 22e - Diabetes Mellitus: Complications (Diabetic Ketoacidosis and Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State)
ADA Standards of Care - Hyperglycemic Crises in Adult Patients with Diabetes 2024
stewardship: Not applicable - non-infective metabolic emergency. Antibiotics only if a precipitating infection is confirmed; empiric cover is not indicated for HHS itself.
contraindications: Avoid rapid osmolality/sodium correction (>3 mmol/L/h fall in effective osmolality risks cerebral oedema)
Do not give insulin before/without commencing fluid resuscitation and checking potassium
Metformin held given AKI; sulfonylurea withheld
edgeCases: Effective osmolality >320 mOsm/kg with glucose usually >33 mmol/L and only mild ketonaemia/acidosis distinguishes HHS from DKA
Mixed HHS/DKA can occur; corrected sodium and calculated osmolality guide fluid strategy
Obtundation should correlate with osmolality - if GCS is low with osmolality <320, seek another cause (stroke, sepsis, drugs)
expectedMaiK: Marked hyperglycaemia with high effective osmolality (>320 mOsm/kg), minimal ketosis and near-normal pH in an obtunded elderly type 2 diabetic indicates hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state, not DKA. Prioritise gradual IV fluid resuscitation with cautious potassium replacement and delayed low-rate insulin, correcting osmolality slowly to avoid cerebral oedema, and actively seek the precipitant (infection, steroids, non-adherence).
expectedNextQuestions: Any recent infection, steroid use, or missed diabetes medication as a precipitant?
Rate and volume of urine output and last oral fluid intake to gauge fluid deficit?
expectedInvestigations: Serial measured/calculated serum osmolality and corrected sodium
Serum/blood ketones and venous blood gas to exclude DKA
Urea, creatinine, potassium with hourly capillary glucose and septic screen for precipitant
regressionAssertions: dka must not rank above hhs given effective osmolality >320 with minimal ketonaemia and near-normal pH
